# Statement of Need (Draft, ~600 words)

*Since I don't know your issue area yet, I've used **[issue]** (e.g., food insecurity, youth mental health, housing instability) and **[service]** (e.g., counseling, case management, job training) as placeholders. Swap them in throughout.*

---

**Statement of Need**

In [City/County], [X%] of [population] experience [issue], a rate [X percentage points / X times] higher than the statewide average of [Y%] [State Health Dept, year]. Nationally, [issue] affects roughly [Z%] of [population] [CDC / national source, year], placing [City/County] well above both state and national benchmarks. These numbers represent [number] of our neighbors, concentrated most heavily in [ZIP codes / neighborhoods], where the rate climbs to [X%] [source, year].

The consequences extend well beyond individual households. [Issue] is closely linked to [related outcome 1, e.g., chronic absenteeism, emergency room use, job loss] and [related outcome 2]. In [City/County], [related outcome] occurs at a rate of [X per 1,000 residents] [source, year], driving up costs for [schools / hospitals / public systems] and limiting residents' ability to [achieve stability / thrive / participate fully in community life].

**Who is affected.** The burden of [issue] falls disproportionately on [primary population, e.g., low-income families, youth ages 12–18, older adults living alone]. In [service area], [X%] of residents live below the federal poverty level, compared with [Y%] statewide [U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates, year]. [X%] are [demographic factor relevant to the need, e.g., Spanish-speaking households, without health insurance, without a vehicle] [source, year]. These residents face compounding barriers: [barrier 1, e.g., limited public transportation], [barrier 2, e.g., few bilingual providers], and [barrier 3, e.g., work schedules that conflict with standard service hours]. As a result, they are least likely to reach existing services even though their need is greatest.

**A growing problem.** [Issue] in [City/County] is not new, but it is getting worse. Since [baseline year], the rate has risen from [X%] to [Y%], an increase of [Z%] [source, year range]. [Optional: Contributing factors include (rising housing costs / the loss of [local employer or program] / post-pandemic effects), which have (pushed more families into crisis / eroded existing supports).] Without intervention, local projections suggest [projected outcome] by [year] [source, if available].

**Gaps in current services.** Existing resources have not kept pace with demand. [City/County] has [number] [providers / programs / slots] offering [service], or one for every [X] residents in need, well short of the recommended ratio of [Y] [professional association or benchmark source, year]. Currently, [number] residents are on waitlists for [service], with an average wait of [weeks/months] [local provider data / 211 call data, year]. [Number] of [City/County]'s [ZIP codes / neighborhoods] have no [service] provider at all. Where services do exist, [limitation, e.g., they are available only in English, require transportation residents lack, or operate only during weekday business hours].

**What the community is telling us.** Residents consistently identify [issue] as a top concern. In a [year] [survey / focus group series / community health needs assessment] of [n] residents, [X%] named [issue] as [one of the most pressing problems / their primary barrier to stability] [source, year]. As one [participant / parent / resident] shared: *"[Short, specific quote describing lived experience of the problem or difficulty accessing help.]"*

**Why now.** [Organization] is positioned to close this gap. The need is documented, the population is identifiable, and the shortage of accessible [service] is clear. The program described in the following sections is designed specifically to reach the residents existing services miss and to reverse the trend of the past [number] years.

---

## 3 Alternate Opening Lines

1. **Data-forward:** "In [City/County], [X] of every 10 [population] [experience issue], nearly [double / X times] the statewide rate [source, year]."
2. **Human-centered:** "Every [week/month], [number] [City/County] [families / youth / residents] [face concrete consequence, e.g., go to bed hungry, are turned away from counseling] because [service] is not available when and where they need it."
3. **Urgency/trend:** "Since [year], [issue] in [City/County] has risen by [X%], outpacing both state and national trends, while the services designed to address it have [stayed flat / declined]."

*Tip:* Option 1 tends to score best with data-focused reviewers. Option 2 works well if the funder emphasizes community voice. Use whichever you can back up with your strongest number.

---

## 6 Local Data Sources to Pull From

| # | Source | What You'll Get | Where/How to Find It |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **U.S. Census Bureau: American Community Survey (ACS)** | Poverty, income, age, race/ethnicity, language, insurance, vehicle access, by county, city, ZIP, or census tract | **data.census.gov**. Search your geography plus a topic (e.g., "poverty [County]"). Use **5-Year Estimates** for ZIP- and tract-level reliability. |
| 2 | **County Health Rankings & Roadmaps** | County-level health outcomes and factors compared with state and national figures; good for benchmarks | **countyhealthrankings.org**. Select your state and county, then download the data file for exact figures and source years. |
| 3 | **Local Hospital Community Health Needs Assessment (CHNA)** | Prioritized community needs, resident survey results, focus group findings; often your best "community voice" source | Nonprofit hospitals must publish these every 3 years. Search "[Hospital name] Community Health Needs Assessment" or check the hospital's website under "Community Benefit." |
| 4 | **CDC PLACES** | Model-based estimates for chronic disease, mental health, and health behaviors at the census tract and ZIP level | **cdc.gov/places**. Use the interactive map or download data for your county or ZIPs. |
| 5 | **211 / United Way Data (including ALICE Report)** | Call volume by need type and ZIP (shows demand and gaps); ALICE shows households above poverty but unable to afford basics | Search "[Your state] 211 counts" or contact your local 211 directly. ALICE reports are at **unitedforalice.org**. |
| 6 | **State Agency Data Portals** (Health, Education, Human Services) | Issue-specific local data: school report cards, SNAP enrollment, behavioral health, housing/homelessness (HUD Point-in-Time counts) | Search "[State] Department of Health data portal" or "[State] school report card." For homelessness, use HUD's **PIT and HIC** data via your local Continuum of Care. |

**Also worth checking for waitlist and gap data:** partner agencies (ask directly for waitlist numbers and average wait times), your own intake records, and local provider directories. Funders value this hyper-local evidence highly because it can't be found elsewhere.

---

If you tell me your issue area and service area, I can tighten the language, point you to the most relevant specific datasets, and suggest which benchmarks reviewers in that field expect to see.

# Program Design & Activities (Draft, ~800 words)

*Note: Now that the issue area is youth literacy, update the Statement of Need placeholders to match (e.g., [X%] of 3rd graders in ZIPs 12345/12346 reading below grade level [State Dept. of Education, year]). The links below assume that section names four needs: **(1) low reading proficiency, (2) limited home literacy resources, (3) summer learning loss, and (4) a shortage of after-school academic support.***

---

**Program Design & Activities**

**Program overview and logic model.** [Program Name] is a year-round literacy program for K–5 students from low-income families in ZIPs 12345 and 12346, with priority enrollment at [School A] and [School B]. Our logic is simple. Students who are behind in reading need more instructional time, delivered in small groups by trained tutors and reinforced at home and over the summer. **Inputs** (trained staff, [University Literacy Corps] volunteers, school and library partnerships, evidence-based curricula) support three core **activities**: small-group tutoring, family literacy nights, and summer reading camps. These produce measurable **outputs** (tutoring sessions delivered, families engaged, books distributed) that lead to **short-term outcomes** (improved foundational reading skills and more reading at home) and **long-term outcomes** (more students reading at grade level by the end of 3rd grade). *A one-page logic model is attached as [Attachment X].*

**Activity 1: Small-Group Tutoring** *(addresses Needs 1 and 4)*
- **What:** Structured, skills-based tutoring in phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension, using [curriculum name].
- **Who:** [X] students per year. Each group of 3–4 students is led by a trained tutor and supervised by a certified reading specialist.
- **Dosage:** Three 45-minute sessions per week for [28] weeks (about 63 instructional hours per student).
- **Location:** On-site at [School A] and [School B], immediately after dismissal, so students need no extra transportation.
- **Evidence:** Small-group, high-frequency tutoring produces significant gains in early reading, especially when it is delivered during or right after the school day by trained tutors [National Bureau of Economic Research tutoring meta-analysis, year]. Explicit instruction in foundational skills is strongly supported for grades K–3 [What Works Clearinghouse Practice Guide, year].

**Activity 2: Family Literacy Nights** *(addresses Need 2)*
- **What:** Interactive sessions where families learn practical strategies for reading together at home (questioning techniques, read-aloud routines, using library resources). Each family leaves with [X] free books.
- **Who:** Families of enrolled students, co-facilitated by Site Coordinators and [Local Library] staff. Interpretation is provided in [language(s)].
- **Dosage:** Monthly 90-minute sessions ([8] per year), with dinner and childcare provided.
- **Location:** Rotating between partner schools and [Local Library branch].
- **Evidence:** Family engagement in literacy activities is associated with stronger reading achievement, particularly when schools provide specific, modeled strategies rather than general encouragement [family literacy research source, year].

**Activity 3: Summer Reading Camp** *(addresses Needs 1 and 3)*
- **What:** A literacy-rich day camp that combines targeted skill instruction with student-chosen reading, library visits, and enrichment activities.
- **Who:** Up to [X] students, prioritizing those who remain below benchmark in spring. Staffed by the reading specialist, Site Coordinators, and Literacy Corps volunteers.
- **Dosage:** Four half-days per week for [5] weeks (about 60 hours).
- **Location:** [School A or B] and [Local Library].
- **Evidence:** Summer reading programs that pair instruction with access to self-selected books reduce summer learning loss among low-income students [summer reading meta-analysis, year].

**Participant pathway.**
1. **Referral:** Classroom teachers refer K–5 students who score below benchmark on the district's [screening tool, e.g., DIBELS 8/i-Ready] in fall.
2. **Intake:** Site Coordinators obtain parent consent, confirm eligibility (school meal eligibility or equivalent), and record baseline scores.
3. **Intervention:** Students are grouped by skill need and begin tutoring within [2] weeks of enrollment. Families are invited to literacy nights.
4. **Progress monitoring:** Tutors assess students every [6] weeks and regroup them as skills change.
5. **Exit:** A student exits when they meet benchmark on two consecutive checks or reach the end of the school year. Spring non-completers are prioritized for summer camp.
6. **Follow-up:** We review fall benchmark data the next school year to measure skill retention and re-enroll students who need continued support.

**Staffing and volunteers.** A **Program Director** ([0.5] FTE) oversees operations, partnerships, and evaluation. A **Reading Specialist** ([1.0] FTE, state-certified) designs instruction, trains tutors, and leads data review. Two **Site Coordinators** ([X] FTE each) manage daily operations, family outreach, and volunteer scheduling. **[University Literacy Corps] volunteers** ([X] per semester) serve as tutors after completing [X] hours of training and receive ongoing coaching. [School District] provides space, screening data under a data-sharing agreement, and teacher referrals.

**Assumptions, risks, and mitigation.**

*Assumptions:*
- Partner schools will provide space and timely access to screening data.
- Families can attend evening events when barriers such as meals, childcare, and language are removed.
- The university will supply enough trained volunteers each semester.

*Risks and mitigation:*
- **Volunteer turnover at semester breaks** → Recruit 20% above need, use semester-long commitments, and keep paid staff as backup tutors.
- **Inconsistent student attendance** → Hold sessions right after dismissal, call families after two absences, and give attendance incentives.
- **Delays in data access** → Execute the data-sharing MOU before launch and run our own baseline assessment at intake as a backup.

---

## Activity–Outcome Table

| Activity | Target Output | Short-Term Outcome | Responsible Staff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small-group tutoring | [X] students receive 60+ hours of tutoring | [X%] of students gain [X] points on [assessment] | Reading Specialist; Literacy Corps tutors |
| Progress monitoring | Assessments every 6 weeks for 100% of enrolled students | Instruction adjusted to student need; [X%] meet benchmark by spring | Reading Specialist |
| Family literacy nights | [8] sessions; [X] families attend at least 3 | [X%] of families report reading together 3+ times per week | Site Coordinators; [Local Library] |
| Home book distribution | [X] books distributed ([X] per child) | More books in the home; increased independent reading | Site Coordinators |
| Summer reading camp | [X] students attend 75%+ of camp days | [X%] maintain or improve spring-to-fall reading scores | Reading Specialist; Program Director |
| Tutor training and coaching | [X] volunteers complete [X] training hours | [X%] of tutors demonstrate fidelity on observation checklist | Reading Specialist; Program Director |

---

## 4 Phrasing Hooks (Exec Summary / Section Intro)

1. "[Program Name] gives K–5 students who are behind in reading the extra instructional time they need, delivered in small groups, reinforced at home, and sustained through the summer."
2. "Each enrolled student receives about 120 hours of targeted literacy instruction per year, nearly [X] additional weeks of reading instruction, at a cost of $[X] per student."
3. "By delivering services on-site at [School A] and [School B] immediately after dismissal, we remove the transportation and scheduling barriers that keep low-income families from existing programs."
4. "Our partnership with [School District], [Local Library], and [University Literacy Corps] connects school-day data, community resources, and trained volunteers into a single, coordinated pathway to grade-level reading."

---

## Suggested Metrics for the Outcomes Section

**Process metrics (implementation)**
1. **Attendance/dosage:** % of enrolled students attending at least 80% of scheduled tutoring sessions (target: [75%]).
2. **Family engagement:** % of enrolled families attending 3 or more literacy nights (target: [60%]).
3. **Fidelity:** % of observed tutoring sessions meeting fidelity standards on the [curriculum] checklist (target: [85%]).

**Outcome metrics (participant change)**
1. **Reading growth:** % of students showing meaningful growth from fall to spring on [DIBELS/i-Ready], e.g., meeting or exceeding their typical annual growth target (target: [70%]).
2. **Benchmark attainment:** % of participating students reading at or above grade-level benchmark by spring (target: [X%], up from a baseline of [Y%]).
3. **Summer retention:** % of summer camp participants who maintain or improve reading scores from spring to fall (target: [80%]).

*Tip:* Confirm which assessment [School District] uses and when its benchmark windows fall (typically fall, winter, and spring). Aligning your measurement points with theirs saves data collection effort and makes your baseline figures credible to reviewers.

---

# Staffing & Implementation Timeline (Draft, ~400 words)

*Note: The timeline assumes a grant start of **[Month 1 = July, year]** so that hiring and training finish before fall screening. If your start date differs, shift the months but keep the sequence: **MOU → hiring → volunteer training → fall screening → intake → launch**.*

---

**Staffing & Implementation Timeline**

[Program Name] will be delivered by a small, experienced core team. Each role is tied directly to one or more program activities.

| Role | FTE | Key Qualifications | Core Responsibilities | Salary Line Item |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Program Director | [0.5] | Master's in education or related field; [5]+ years managing youth programs; experience with school partnerships | Oversees operations, partnerships, budget, evaluation, and reporting; supervises all staff | $[X] + fringe [X%] |
| Reading Specialist | [1.0] | State reading specialist certification; [3]+ years of K–5 literacy instruction; training in [curriculum] | Designs instruction, trains and coaches tutors, leads progress monitoring and data review, directs summer camp instruction | $[X] + fringe [X%] |
| Site Coordinator ([School A]) | [X] | Bachelor's degree preferred; experience with youth and families; [language] proficiency preferred | Manages daily site operations, attendance, family outreach, literacy nights, and volunteer scheduling | $[X] + fringe [X%] |
| Site Coordinator ([School B]) | [X] | Same as above | Same as above | $[X] + fringe [X%] |
| Volunteer Tutors ([University Literacy Corps]) | [X] volunteers/semester | Enrolled students; cleared background check; completion of [12]-hour pre-service training | Deliver small-group tutoring and support summer camp | In-kind ($[X] value) / stipend $[X] |

**Supervision.** The Program Director supervises the Reading Specialist and Site Coordinators and meets with them weekly. The Reading Specialist provides instructional supervision of all tutors. Site Coordinators handle logistics, scheduling, and attendance. The full team holds a data meeting every two weeks to review attendance and progress-monitoring results and adjust student groupings.

**Volunteer onboarding and coaching.** Each volunteer completes a background check and clearances required by [School District], mandated-reporter training, and [12] hours of pre-service training in [curriculum] and small-group management. Tutors then receive:
- monthly group coaching sessions,
- two fidelity observations per semester using the [curriculum] checklist, and
- individual feedback within one week of each observation.

Tutors who fall below fidelity standards receive targeted re-coaching and a follow-up observation.

**Implementation Timeline: Months 1–9**

| Month | Milestones |
|---|---|
| 1 ([July]) | Execute MOU and data-sharing agreement with [School District]; post Reading Specialist and Site Coordinator positions |
| 2 ([August]) | Hire Reading Specialist and Site Coordinators; finalize space-use agreements; begin volunteer recruitment with [University Literacy Corps] |
| 3 ([September]) | Complete staff onboarding; volunteer background checks and pre-service training; district fall screening; teacher referrals begin |
| 4 ([October]) | Intake and parent consent; baseline assessment; **first cohort launches** at both sites; first family literacy night |
| 5 ([November]) | **First progress review** (6-week assessment); regroup students; first fidelity observations |
| 6 ([December]) | Mid-year staff and volunteer check-in; recruit spring-semester volunteers; second literacy night |
| 7 ([January]) | Spring volunteer training; district winter benchmark; second progress review |
| 8 ([February]) | Fidelity observations; mid-year report to funder; family survey (mid-point) |
| 9 ([March]) | Third progress review; begin summer camp planning and enrollment priorities |

*Months 10–12:* spring benchmark, tutoring wraps up, summer camp launches ([June]), and the year-end evaluation and annual report are completed.

**Startup budget notes.** Year 1 personnel costs reflect staggered hiring, with partial-year salaries for positions filled in Month 2 ($[X]). Startup costs also include recruitment and advertising ($[X]), background checks and clearances for staff and volunteers ($[X]), pre-service training materials and trainer time ($[X]), curriculum and assessment licenses ($[X]), and an initial book inventory for distribution ($[X]). Ongoing years will not repeat most of these one-time costs, which lowers the cost per student after Year 1.

---

## 6 Job-Description Bullets: Reading Specialist

- Design and adapt small-group literacy instruction aligned with [curriculum] and the science of reading for students in grades K–5.
- Deliver [12]-hour pre-service training and monthly coaching for volunteer tutors; conduct fidelity observations and provide written feedback.
- Administer and analyze baseline and progress-monitoring assessments every 6 weeks; regroup students based on skill data.
- Lead biweekly data meetings with Site Coordinators and report student progress to the Program Director and partner schools.
- Develop the summer reading camp curriculum and lead instruction during camp.
- Co-design family literacy night content with [Local Library] staff, modeling practical at-home reading strategies.

---

## 4 Internal Performance-Monitoring Milestones

1. **Readiness by Month 3:** All core staff hired and 100% of volunteers cleared and trained before intake begins.
2. **Enrollment by Month 4:** At least [90%] of target enrollment ([X] students) consented and baseline-assessed within 4 weeks of referrals opening.
3. **Fidelity by Month 5:** At least [85%] of first-round tutor observations meet fidelity standards, with re-coaching completed for those who do not.
4. **Mid-year progress by Month 7:** At least [50%] of students on track to meet their annual growth target at the winter benchmark, with an intervention plan documented for students who are off track.

# Outcomes & Objectives (Draft)

*Note: Measurement points align with [School District]'s benchmark windows (fall, winter, spring) and with the 6-week progress-monitoring cycle in the timeline. Confirm the district's assessment and window dates before finalizing targets.*

---

## SMART Objectives with Measurement Notes

**Objective 1: Reading Growth**
By [May, year], at least **[70%]** of students who attend 80% or more of tutoring sessions will meet or exceed their expected annual growth target in reading on [i-Ready / DIBELS 8], compared with a baseline of **[Y%]** of similar students at [School A] and [School B] in [prior year] [School District data, year].

*Measurement tool and timing:* We will use the district's existing screener, [i-Ready Diagnostic / DIBELS 8], which provides norm-referenced growth targets (e.g., i-Ready Typical Growth or DIBELS 8 Zones of Growth). Fall scores collected at intake (Month 4) serve as each student's baseline. Winter scores (Month 7) serve as a mid-year check, and spring scores (Month 10–11) are the exit measure. The baseline comparison comes from the prior-year growth rate for students who scored below benchmark at the same schools, obtained through the data-sharing agreement. Results are reported separately for students meeting the 80% attendance threshold, which lets us connect dosage to growth.

**Objective 2: Benchmark Attainment**
By [May, year], at least **[40%]** of participating students who scored below grade-level benchmark at fall intake will score at or above benchmark on the spring [i-Ready / DIBELS 8] assessment, compared with **[Y%]** of below-benchmark non-participants at the same schools [School District data, year].

*Measurement tool and timing:* This objective uses the same assessment and benchmark windows as Objective 1. Because every student enters the program below benchmark, the participant baseline at intake is near 0% by design. A meaningful comparison therefore needs an external reference. We will use the spring benchmark attainment rate for below-benchmark students at [School A] and [School B] who did not participate, or the prior-year rate if current comparison data are unavailable. The 6-week progress checks (Months 5, 7, and 9) track whether students are on course, but only the spring district benchmark counts toward this objective.

**Objective 3: Summer Learning Retention**
By [October, year+1], at least **[80%]** of students who attend 75% or more of summer camp days will maintain or improve their reading scores from spring to fall, compared with a baseline of **[Y%]** of below-benchmark students at partner schools who did not attend camp [School District data, year].

*Measurement tool and timing:* The spring district benchmark (Month 10–11) is the pre-camp baseline, and the following fall's district screening (September–October of the next school year) is the post-camp measure. "Maintained" means a fall score at or above the student's spring score, using the assessment's scale score. Because the fall data arrive after the grant year ends, we will request them under the data-sharing agreement and report them in the next annual report or as an addendum. We will also give a brief camp-entry and camp-exit skills check to provide immediate feedback.

**Objective 4: Family Reading at Home**
By [May, year], at least **[60%]** of families who attend three or more literacy nights will report reading with their child at least three times per week, up from a baseline of **[Y%]** at intake.

*Measurement tool and timing:* We will use a short family reading survey of 6–8 items, adapted from [validated home literacy environment measure, source], offered in [languages]. Families complete it at intake (Month 4) as the baseline, at mid-year (Month 8) as a check, and in spring (Month 10) as the exit measure. Site Coordinators administer it in person at enrollment and literacy nights, with phone or text follow-up for families who miss events. Matched pre/post responses for the same families are analyzed. Because self-reported reading frequency can be inflated, we will also track library card sign-ups and checkouts through [Local Library] as a supporting indicator.

*Process metrics (attendance, family engagement, fidelity) belong in the Evaluation Plan as implementation measures. They support these outcome objectives but are not outcomes themselves.*

---

## Paste-Ready Draft (Two Sample Objectives)

**Outcomes & Objectives**

[Program Name] will measure success by the change in students' reading skills, not just the services we deliver. Our objectives use [School District]'s existing [i-Ready / DIBELS 8] assessment, so results are comparable to district benchmarks and require no additional student testing.

**Objective 1:** By [May, year], at least [70%] of students attending 80% or more of tutoring sessions will meet or exceed their expected annual growth target in reading on [assessment], compared with a baseline of [Y%] among similar students at [School A] and [School B] in [prior year] [School District data, year].

**Objective 2:** By [October, year+1], at least [80%] of students attending 75% or more of summer reading camp will maintain or improve their reading scores from spring to fall, compared with [Y%] of below-benchmark students at partner schools who did not attend [School District data, year].

---

**Tips on setting targets:**
- Ask the district for last year's growth and benchmark rates at [School A] and [School B] first, then set targets 10–20 points above that baseline. Reviewers look for targets that are ambitious but defensible.
- Use the same numbers in the Executive Summary, the Activity–Outcome table, and the Evaluation Plan. Inconsistent figures across sections are a common scoring deduction.

Next is the **Evaluation Plan**: design, data collection schedule, who analyzes the data, and how findings feed back into the program. Want me to draft it?

# Evaluation Plan (Draft, ~500 words)

*Note: This plan adds a **Data & Evaluation Coordinator** ([0.25] FTE), which was not in the staffing table. Add that row to the Staffing section and budget, or assign these duties to the Program Director with support from an external evaluator (see the budget note below).*

---

**Evaluation Plan**

**Design.** [Program Name] will use a **quasi-experimental pre/post design with a comparison group**. Participants are K–5 students at [School A] and [School B] who score below benchmark in fall and enroll in the program. The comparison group is made up of below-benchmark students at the same schools who do not enroll, matched on grade, fall baseline score, and [meal eligibility / English learner status]. If too few non-participants are available, we will use prior-year below-benchmark students at the same schools as a historical comparison. Because families choose to enroll, results will show strong evidence of association rather than proof of causation. Matching on baseline scores reduces, but does not eliminate, selection bias.

**Data sources.** We will draw on four sources:
- [School District]'s [i-Ready / DIBELS 8] benchmark assessments (fall, winter, spring)
- Program progress monitoring every 6 weeks
- Attendance logs for tutoring, literacy nights, and summer camp
- Family and student surveys

Supporting data include tutor fidelity observations and library card and checkout data from [Local Library].

**Data management and analysis.** The Data & Evaluation Coordinator maintains the program database, cleans and merges district and program data, and produces dashboards for biweekly team data meetings. The Reading Specialist oversees assessment quality, and the Program Director is accountable for evaluation and reporting. [An external evaluator, [Name/Firm], will finalize the comparison-group design, conduct the annual outcome analysis, and review the year-end report.]

**Privacy and data-sharing safeguards.** Student data will be shared under a written data-sharing agreement with [School District] that complies with FERPA. Parents will consent to data use at intake. Safeguards include:
- Students are identified by coded IDs, with the key stored separately.
- Data are stored on encrypted, password-protected systems with role-based access.
- No identifiable data leave secure systems.
- Results are reported only in aggregate, with groups smaller than [10] suppressed.
- Data are destroyed or returned according to the agreement's timeline.

If [University] faculty or students analyze data for research, we will obtain IRB review before any data are shared.

**Reporting cadence.**
- *Internal:* biweekly data meetings
- *Partners:* quarterly dashboard to [School District] principals and [Local Library]
- *Funder:* mid-year report (Month 8) and annual report (Month 12), plus a fall addendum with summer-retention results
- *Families:* an annual plain-language summary in [languages]

**Continuous improvement.** We will use set decision rules so that data lead to action:
- **No growth across two consecutive progress checks:** The student is regrouped, receives added sessions, or is reviewed by the Reading Specialist.
- **Site attendance below [70%] for four weeks:** The site triggers a family outreach plan.
- **Tutor fidelity below [85%]:** The tutor receives re-coaching and a follow-up observation.

Each quarter, we will break results down by school, grade, and language to catch gaps early and adjust the program.

**Evaluation budget.** A commonly cited guideline is to spend **5–10% of the total program budget** on evaluation. We recommend a **hybrid model**: program staff handle routine data collection, and an external evaluator ($[X], about [X]% of the budget) designs the comparison analysis and validates annual results. Reviewers often see an external evaluator as a sign of objectivity. A lower-cost option is a partnership with [University] education faculty.

## 6 Sample Survey Items

**Family survey** (offered in [languages])
1. In the past 7 days, on how many days did you or another adult read with your child? *(0 / 1–2 / 3–4 / 5–7 days)*
2. About how many children's books are in your home? *(0–10 / 11–25 / 26–50 / more than 50)*
3. How confident do you feel helping your child with reading at home? *(1 = Not at all confident to 5 = Very confident)*
4. Does your child have a public library card? *(Yes / No / Not sure)*

**Student survey** (read aloud for grades K–2, with a 3-face 😀 😐 ☹️ response scale)

5. "I like reading books."
6. "When I get to a word I don't know, I can figure it out."

*Tip: Consider adapting items from an established instrument such as the Elementary Reading Attitude Survey [McKenna & Kear, 1990] so reviewers see a validated basis for your measure.*

## Suggested Analysis Methods by Objective

| Objective | Primary Analysis | Supporting Analysis |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Reading growth** | Percent of students meeting their annual growth target; compare participants with the comparison group using a chi-square test or logistic regression that controls for baseline score and grade | **Dose-response regression:** growth (or meeting the target) predicted by hours attended, controlling for baseline score; paired t-test on fall-to-spring scale scores |
| **2. Benchmark attainment** | Percent of participants at or above spring benchmark compared with matched non-participants (chi-square or logistic regression) | Results broken down by grade, school, and English learner status |
| **3. Summer retention** | Percent of campers who maintain or improve from spring to fall, compared with non-camp students | Paired t-test on spring-to-fall scores (see the caution below) |
| **4. Family reading** | Percent reporting reading 3+ days per week, intake vs. spring; **McNemar's test** for matched yes/no responses | Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the full frequency scale; library checkout trends |
| **Process metrics** | Descriptive statistics: attendance rates, percent of families attending 3+ events, percent of observations meeting fidelity | Tracked quarterly by site |

**Two analysis cautions:**
- **Grade-level scoring:** i-Ready scale scores are on a single scale across grades, so spring-to-fall comparisons work directly. DIBELS 8 composite scores are grade-specific, so for Objective 3 you should compare benchmark status or percentile rank rather than raw composites. Confirm which assessment the district uses.
- **Small samples:** With fewer than about 30 students per group, significance tests may be underpowered. Report effect sizes and descriptive results alongside p-values so reviewers can see the size of the gains.
